manufacturer.triumph-adler.description: German office-machine and computer manufacturer whose Dario systems shared their engineering with Olivetti PCS models during the Olivetti ownership period.
manufacturer.triumph-adler.history:
Triumph-Adler brings together two German industrial histories. Triumph began in Nuremberg in 1896 as a bicycle maker, while Adler had started producing typewriters there at the end of the nineteenth century. The two companies later met in the office market: typewriters, calculators and their sales networks were their starting point, rather than a computing tradition created from nothing.

By the late 1960s the group had entered office electronics with the TA 100. The TA 10 of 1971 brought programming into a typewriter-like format and was presented by the company as a “people’s computer” for offices. The Alphatronic microcomputer family opened another chapter in 1979: instead of merely automating one office task, it offered a personal-computer platform. That path explains why the brand continued to coexist with typing and document-management businesses.

Volkswagen acquired a majority holding in 1979 and sold the company to Olivetti in 1986. The transaction gave the Italian company a German subsidiary with its own development, production and channels; it did not turn Triumph-Adler’s earlier computers into Olivetti designs retrospectively. During that period, the Dario desktops—also sold as the P35 and P45—were closely related to Olivetti’s PCS machines. BluMach keeps the Dario 286 and Dario 386SX as distinct records: documentation and firmware can demonstrate a shared platform without erasing the commercial identity of either machine.

Triumph-Adler also introduced the Walkstation 286 and 386 notebooks in 1990. Following restructuring in 1991, it returned chiefly to operating as a sales company. Later ownership changes and acquisitions moved the business towards office communications, printing and document management. Since 2010, TA Triumph-Adler and its UTAX brand have belonged to the Kyocera Group. Its story therefore links the mechanical desk, the microcomputer and today’s digital document management.
